paper_title: Eat Your Precision: Precision Objective Mitigates Reward Hacking in Rubric-based RL

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Rubric-based rewards enable effective reinforcement learning on non-verifiable tasks. However, because these rewards are typically defined as a weighted measure of rubric coverage, models are trained primarily to maximize a recall objective. As a result, RL-trained models produce responses that are more complete but also more verbose and contain more unnecessary or factually incorrect content, leading them to be less preferred than responses from the base model. To address this issue, we present the FORK reward, which jointly optimizes recall and a novel precision objective, which requires each unit of a model response to be both necessary and factually correct, as measured by rubric-driven necessity credits and a factual-correctness grader, respectively. Our experimental results show that FORK outperforms existing rubric-based RL methods and achieves Pareto-optimal performance that balances rubric coverage and overall response quality. Compared to the original recall-based reward, FORK substantially improves precision and reduces response length while achieving similar rubric coverage, which leads to significantly higher win rate compared to the base policy (e.g., from 10.6% to 68.0% on RubricHub-Medical and from 22.1% to 74.1% on HealthBench).

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards has led to rapid advances in AI for math and coding, where the correctness of the answers can be reliably measured and used as reward signals. In comparison, for non-verifiable tasks such as open-ended generation, the evaluation criteria for model responses can be diverse and sometimes subjective, which makes it difficult to define rewards in RL. To resolve this issue, Gunjal et al. (2026) and Viswanathan et al. (2026) leverage rubricbased RL, which first generates set of rubrics that model responses should satisfy and then uses the weighted coverage of these pre-defined rubrics as rewards. However, such rubric-coverage-based reward is easily hacked. As shown in Figure 1, when model is only optimized towards maximizing the coverage of pre-defined rubrics, we observe that although the model responses become more complete, their factual correctness and necessity decrease, and the responses become more verbose. This makes them less preferred than base policy responses (Mahmoud et al., 2026). This reward hacking behavior is not surprising since rubrics as rewards currently behave like recall objective. The missing part is precision objective: whether the content of model response is factually correct and necessary. With this motivation, we propose FORK, which converts rubric-based rewards from recall score into an Fβ score that aggregates recall and precision via their weighted harmonic mean. Given set of rubrics, to measure the precision, we first divide model response into sequence of units and then determine the necessity and factual correctness of each unit by prompting an LLM grader. With the standard coverage reward, recall (i.e., weighted coverage of rubrics) quickly saturates, while precision and win rate against base model continually decreases and responses become more verbose. With precision objective included in the reward (FORK), the model reaches similar recall while gradually increasing precision and win rate and generating less verbose responses. Here, we train Qwen2.57B-Instruct on RubricHub-Medical and evaluate it on an in-domain test set. credit-based method in which an LLM grader matches rubrics to units, assigns each unit necessity credit, and determines unit necessity based on dynamic threshold value. We demonstrate the effectiveness of FORK on both in-domain datasets (the test splits of RubricHubMedical and RubricHub-Science, Li et al. (2026)) and external benchmarks (HealthBench, Arora et al. (2025) and ResearchQA, Yifei et al. (2026)). Compared to the standard coverage reward, FORK significantly improves the factual correctness and necessity of responses (e.g., reducing the response length by factor of 2.6) while maintaining similar rubric coverage. These improvements also make responses from rubric-based RL-trained models more preferred than base policy responses. Further analysis supports the effectiveness of FORK. While rubric-coverage rewards (Gunjal et al., 2026; Rezaei et al., 2025; Viswanathan et al., 2026) have negative effect on satisfaction of absencebased rubrics, our method improves satisfaction of both presence-based and absence-based rubrics, enabling models to add necessary content and suppress irrelevant content at the same time. We also verify that model trained with our method remains preferred to the base model under different judge prompts and remains more effective than other rubric-based RL methods when evaluated with different LLM graders. Our key contributions are: 1. We propose FORK, which mitigates reward hacking in rubric-based RL training by incorporating precision objective into standard coverage objective. 2. We develop reliable method for using an LLM grader to measure the precision of free-form responses given set of rubrics to be satisfied. 3. Experiments show that on multiple public benchmarks, compared to the standard coverage reward, FORK significantly improves precision while maintaining similar rubric coverage, which leads to substantial improvements in the preference score (i.e., win rate compared to the base policy). FORK also outperforms other rubric-based RL methods, achieving Pareto-optimal performance that balances rubric coverage and overall response quality.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORKS
sections.content: Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning. Rubric-based methods decompose response quality into explicit, prompt-specific criteria, providing structured supervision for tasks without readily verifiable outcomes (Gunjal et al., 2026; Viswanathan et al., 2026). Rubrics as Rewards uses expertguided, instance-specific rubrics as on-policy RL rewards, exploring both explicit aggregation of criterion scores and implicit aggregation by an LLM grader (Gunjal et al., 2026). Reinforcement Learning from Checklist Feedback (RLCF) evaluates instruction-specific requirements using LLM graders and specialized verification programs, and converts aggregated checklist scores into preference pairs for direct preference optimization (Viswanathan et al., 2026). RubricHub scales rubric supervision through coarse-to-fine generation that combines principle-guided synthesis, multi-model aggregation, and difficulty evolution, supporting rubric-based RL (Li et al., 2026). These methods establish rubrics as practical interface for specifying training objectives. We build on this paradigm while distinguishing coverage of specified requirements from the quality of all generated content.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Rubric Specification and Reward Hacking. Rubric-based optimization remains vulnerable to incomplete reward specifications. Mahmoud et al. (2026) distinguish verifier failure from rubricdesign limitations: even with strong verification, rubric-based judges can prefer RL-trained responses that rubric-free judges rate worse overall, with improved completeness but degraded factual correctness and necessity. Several approaches address insufficiently specified requirements. RLCF adds universal criteria against excessive or off-topic content after observing verbose preambles under checklist optimization (Viswanathan et al., 2026). Zhang et al. (2026) refine rubrics by contrasting high-quality, diverse responses, improving discrimination in the high-reward region and delaying over-optimization. OnlineRubrics augments existing criteria through comparisons between current-policy and control-policy responses (Rezaei et al., 2025). DR Tulu maintains searchgrounded, evolving rubrics that capture both newly discovered useful content and undesirable behaviors observed in rollouts (Shao et al., 2025). AMARIS further uses persistent training diagnostics to revise criteria and weights in response to recurring failures (Wu et al., 2026). These specificationrefinement strategies motivate complementary question: how should generated content be evaluated when coverage requirements remain incomplete? Our method supplements rubric coverage with unit-level assessments of necessity and factual correctness, rather than relying on criterion expansion alone, and does not require online rubric updates. Fine-Grained Evaluation and PrecisionRecall Rewards. Content-level evaluation provides complementary perspective on response quality. Min et al. (2023) measure factual precision as the proportion of generated atomic facts supported by reliable knowledge source. Song et al. (2024) combine sentence-level faithfulness assessment with keyfactsentence alignment to measure completeness and conciseness, distinguishing coverage of target information from the fraction of generated sentences contributing that information. Related work directly incorporates precision recall signals into policy optimization. Jhaveri et al. (2025) train clinical note generators with claim-level F1 reward combining entailment-based precision against the source dialogue and recall over dialogue-derived claims. For video captioning, Gao et al. (2026) verify atomic claims against video evidence and balance factual precision with reference-claim coverage, assigning attenuated credit to supported but unmatched details and bounding their contribution to recall. Our work adapts this content-level perspective to rubric-based RL: necessity is derived from units contribution to prompt-specific coverage requirements, and precision counts units that satisfy both necessity and factual correctness. Combining this precision with rubric-coverage recall through an Fβ reward couples what response should cover with whether its generated content is warranted and correct.

sections.title: 3 FORK: PRECISION-AWARE RUBRIC REWARD
sections.content: In this section, we propose FORK, which can mitigate reward hacking in rubric-based RL by incorporating precision objective (Figure 2). We first provide background on the standard rubric-coverage reward formulation (Section 3.1), describe how to measure the precision of model responses (Section 3.2), and introduce FORK as new reward formulation for rubric-based RL (Section 3.3).

We preserve the original wording and substantive content, making only minimal substitutions needed to make each unit self-contained. sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: Our experiments address four research questions: (RQ1) Can FORK improve response precision and overall quality while maintaining comparable rubric coverage? (RQ2) Do these improvements generalize to external benchmarks? (RQ3) How do precision estimation and precisionrecall aggregation affect performance? (RQ4) Are the observed improvements robust to changes in evaluation graders and judge prompts?

sections.title: 4.1 SETUP
sections.content: Base Model and Datasets. We mainly use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2025) as the base policy model, following previous rubric-based RL work (Gunjal et al., 2026; Rezaei et al., 2025; Mahmoud et al., 2026). We separately train the model on two subsets of RubricHub (Li et al., 2026), Medical and Science. Each example consists of prompt (or query) sourced from existing open-ended QA datasets and set of evaluation rubrics and their weights R(x) synthesized through multiple steps using LLMs. In our experiments, for the Science subset, we exclude examples sourced from ResearchQA (Yifei et al., 2026) to use this benchmark as separate evaluation suite. As result, the Medical subset contains 12,519 training examples and 1,391 test examples, and the Science subset contains 19,806 training examples and 2,201 test examples.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Baselines and Ablations. Based on their reward formulations, we categorize other methods designed to mitigate reward hacking in rubric-based RL into the following three types: (1) Rubric-Coverage Rewards include OnlineRubrics (Rezaei et al., 2025), which adds complementary rubrics to predefined rubrics at every training step by comparing current-policy and controlpolicy responses; Universal Rubrics6, which adds two generic criteria (necessity and factual correctness) to the predefined rubrics; and Reweighted Absence-Based Rubrics, which increases the weights wj of absence-based rubrics. We also include the Standard rubric-coverage reward (Gunjal et al., 2026) for reference. (2) Preference-Based Rewards include Holistic Preference7, which assigns rewards according to an LLM graders overall preference based on rubric coverage, necessity, and factual correctness when comparing current-policy and control-policy responses. If current-policy response is preferred, the reward is 1; if it is less preferred, the reward is 0; and if the responses are tied, the reward is 0.5. (3) Ablations: FORK Rewards with Precision Variants include Generic Criteria, which measures precision as the fraction of necessary and factually correct units, both determined by prompting an LLM grader; Offline Criteria, which elicits prompt-specific precision criteria by comparing different model responses before training; and Online Criteria, which elicits precision criteria specific to current-policy responses at each training step. For simplicity, we use base policy responses as control-policy responses. Implementation details for the baselines and ablations we introduce are provided in Appendix A, and their corresponding training prompts are provided in Appendix E.1. Training Grader Selection. We select an LLM to use as the training grader for all rubric-based RL experiments. To do that, we first select five candidate training graders and measure agreements of their judgments with three frontier models. The result shows that Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026b) shows the strongest correlation (r = 0.714), so we use this model as universal training grader. Please refer to Appendix for the detailed grader selection process. Evaluation. We evaluate in-domain performance on RubricHub test sets and cross-dataset generalization on external benchmarks (i.e., HealthBench (Arora et al., 2025) for the medical domain and ResearchQA (Yifei et al., 2026) for the science domain). We conduct two types of evaluations: (1) rubric-based evaluations measuring macro rubric recall, macro precision, and macro F1, and (2) rubric-free evaluations reporting the overall win rate against the base policy model and average response length (i.e., verbosity). We use GPT-5.4 (Singh et al., 2025), strong frontier LLM, as reference grader for automating these evaluations. We use the same rubric-free judge prompt as in Mahmoud et al. (2026) and provide newly introduced judge prompts in Appendix E.2. To measure precision, reference grader directly determines unit necessity and factual correctness given set of coverage rubrics. We compute the F1 score as the harmonic mean of rubric recall and precision. Hyperparameters and Implementation Details. We update the policy model using the group relative policy optimization (GRPO) algorithm (Shao et al., 2024) with 16 rollouts per prompt, context length of 2,000 tokens, and sampling temperature of 1.0. Models are trained with batch size of 128, learning rate of 4.2 106, and constant schedule with 5% linear warmup for 3 epochs on 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs.

sections.title: 4.3 ANALYSIS
sections.content: Improvement in satisfaction of both presenceand absence-based rubrics. In RubricHub, most of the coverage reward weight falls on presence-based rubrics rather than absence-based rubrics (Mahmoud et al., 2026). Accordingly, we observe that the standard coverage reward significantly increases the presence-based rubric satisfaction rate (+15.0 pp) while slightly decreasing the absence-based rubric satisfaction rate (-3.2 pp)  (Table 3)  . This implies that the model learns to add both desirable and undesirable content. Rubric-coverage reward baselines produce more desirable content but fail to suppress undesirable content. In contrast, our method nearly matches the presence-based rubric satisfaction rate of the standard coverage reward while improving the absence-based rubric satisfaction rate (+5.7 pp). Robustness to rubric-free evaluation judge prompts. Since rubric-free win rates depend heavily on LLM judge prompt instructions, we verify whether our method is robust to prompt variations. To do so, we adopt another judge prompt from Rezaei et al. (2025) and verify on the medical domain  (Table 4)  . Since rubric-coverage reward baselines have significantly degraded win rates, we do not include those results. Our method mostly outperforms the other baselines on both evaluation suites, supporting its robustness to different judge prompts. Isolating the effectiveness of our reward formulation. We use reference grader for our main evaluation (Section 4.2). However, this evaluation combines the effect of our reward formulation with the effect of transferring to stronger, unseen grader. To isolate the former, we use the training grader for evaluation (Figure 3). The results show that FORK rewards have the highest win rates among rubric-based RL methods, while β = 1.25 shows Pareto-optimal performance that balances rubric coverage and overall win rate. This supports the effectiveness of our reward formulation compared to the baselines. Different precisionrecall aggregations. To justify using harmonic mean to aggregate precision and recall, we compare F1 score aggregation with simple averaging  (Table 6)  . The results show that simple averaging yields slightly higher precision (+2.1 pp) but lower recall (-6.3 pp) than F1 score aggregation. We observe that higher precision compensates for lower rubric recall during training. We also investigate whether further increasing the weight of recall in Fβ score aggregation is beneficial. To do so, we train model with F2 score aggregation but observe detrimental effect on both precision and recall. We leave finding the optimal value of β for future work. Our unit necessity prediction outperforms prompting-based method. To measure the accuracy of unit necessity prediction, we progressively remove units predicted as unnecessary from response and measure how much rubric recall score is decreased (Figure 4). sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: In this work, we introduce FORK, simple method that mitigates reward hacking in rubric-based RL, by adding complementary precision objective to the original recall-based reward. To address the observed reward hacking behavior, we define precision objective to require each unit of model response to be necessary and factually correct. We propose rubric-driven necessity credits to faithfully measure necessity and use an LLM grader to measure factual correctness. Our experimental results show that FORK outperforms other rubric-based RL methods and achieves Pareto-optimal performance that balances recall and overall response quality.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: In this work, we used generative AI tools for searching related previous works and checking grammar. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work. Specifically, we manually looked at the previous works that the AI tool suggests and verified their relevance. sections.content: A DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF OTHER RUBRIC-BASED RL METHODS In Section 4.1, we briefly describe which baselines and ablations we adopt. Since there are newly introduced methods, in this section, we further describe how those are implemented in detail. A.1 RUBRIC-COVERAGE REWARDS Universal Rubrics adds two generic rubrics corresponds to necessity and factual correctness to predefined set of rubrics. The verbatim rubrics are: (1) The model response should be necessary: every part is needed, with nothing repeated, padded, tangential, or included only to sound thorough., (2) The model response should be factually correct: every claim is correct and supported, with nothing fabricated, misleading, or overconfident.. Reweighted Absence-Based Rubrics first determines absence-based rubrics. If rubric contains both presence-based component and absence-based component, we consider it as an absence-based. Then, given these absence-based rubrics and their original weights, an LLM increases their weights. The prompt is provided in Figure 1011. A.2 PREFERENCE-BASED REWARDS Holistic Preference let an LLM grader to decide its preference of current policy responses against base policy responses and uses as reward. The prompt is provided in Figure 1213. A.3 ABLATIONS: FORK REWARDS WITH PRECISION VARIANTS These rewards use the same structure of reward as our method with F1 aggregation, but use different methods of measuring precision. Generic Criteria replaces our credit-based necessity prediction to simple prompting method. Therefore, an LLM grader is given set of response units and corresponding rubrics and determines each units necessity and factual correctness, respectively. The prompt is provided in Figure 14. Offline Criteria generates prompt-specific precision criteria and use those for measuring precision, instead of using two generic criteria, necessity and factual correctness. To generate those criteria, an LLM grader is given two responses, one from base policy model and another from RL-trained policy model with standard coverage reward, and then generates precision criteria by comparing those two responses. During online RL training, these precision criteria are used for every training step. The prompt is provided in Figure 1516. Online Criteria also generates prompt-specific precision criteria but updates those at every training step. To do that, an LLM grader is given current policy response and set of rubrics, and generates online precision criteria by evaluating the response quality. During online RL training, these precision criteria are updated for every training step. The prompt is provided in Figure 1718.

sections.title: B DETAILED TRAINING GRADER SELECTION PROCESS
sections.content: We select an LLM to use as the training grader for all rubric-based RL experiments. This is especially important for mitigating misaligned decisions by the training grader, which have been identified as another mode of reward hacking in rubric-based RL (Mahmoud et al., 2026). We first select candidate training graders as follows: gpt-oss-20b, gpt-oss-120b (Agarwal et al., 2025), GPT-4.1 Mini (Achiam et al., 2023), Qwen3.5-122B-A10B (Qwen Team, 2026a), and Qwen3.635B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026b). Then, using 40 randomly sampled base policy responses from RubricHub-Medical, we measure each training graders ability to make five types of judgments required by our method and the baselines: rubric satisfaction, holistic preference, necessity, factual correctness, and necessity credit thresholding. To do this, we collect judgments from three frontier LLMs, GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, 2026), Gemini 3.8 Flash (Google DeepMind, 2026), and Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic, 2026), take their majority judgments as reference judgments, and measure Pearson correlations between candidate and reference judgments.

sections.title: D QUALITATIVE ANALYSIS OF MODEL RESPONSES
sections.content: On RubricHub-Medical, FORK (β = 1.25) shortens model responses by factor of 2.1 relative to the standard coverage reward while keeping recall nearly the same  (Table 1)  , supporting that verbosity issue is reduced significantly. To qualitatively verify this, we first select two pairs of examples from medical and science domain, where each pair consists of model responses from the standard coverage reward and the proposed FORK reward. Then, we highlight necessary units using reference grader (i.e., GPT-5.4).

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: We confirm that our method mostly generates necessary contents whereas the standard coverage reward does not. Also, while having similar amount of necessary contents, our method generates significantly shorter, more concise responses. One thing we observe in the medical example is that the model trained with the standard coverage reward first generates an initial response, add another response, and repeat this process (Each response ends with: If you have any more questions or need further assistance, feel free to ask. Stay Well! Qwen). Our model does not show this behavior. The science example shows different failure: after computing the work correctly, the standard coverage reward adds verification step that contradicts its own result. The reference grader labels the whole step unnecessary, so none of it is highlighted. The response then concludes that the assumption in the verification step is incorrect, and thus maintain the original answer. Our model does not show this behavior.

sections.content: D.1 MEDICAL: CONSUMER HEALTH QUESTION Prompt Do allergies cause coughing? had bad cough all winter, and it went away for couple months when the weather got warmer. It just started again since the weather has gotten very hot (90 degrees) and rainy. Is there cough medicine for coughs due to allergies? FORK (ours) Yes, allergies can indeed cause coughing, and your symptoms align with this possibility. Allergies can trigger cough through several mechanisms, including: 1. Postnasal Drip: When allergens like pollen, dust mites, or mold irritate the nasal passages, they can cause increased mucus production. This excess mucus can drip down the back of the throat (postnasal drip), stimulating the cough reflex, especially at night or when lying down. 2. Inflammation and Irritation: Allergic reactions can cause inflammation in the airways, which can lead to dry, hacking cough, especially if the airways are sensitive to the allergens. 3. Bronchospasm: In some cases, allergies can cause the airways to narrow, leading to wheezing and coughing, which is more common in individuals with asthma that is triggered by allergies. The pattern you describedcoughing worsening in the winter and returning with hot, rainy weathersuggests that your cough may be related to seasonal allergies, possibly to mold, pollen, or other outdoor allergens that are more prevalent in these conditions, or to indoor allergens that may be more active in warmer, humid weather (like dust mites, mold, or pet dander). Cough Medicines for Allergy-Induced Cough There are several types of cough medicines that can help manage allergy-induced cough, but its important to note that they should be used under the guidance of healthcare provider, especially if you have underlying health conditions or are taking other medications. Here are some options: 1. Antihistamines: These can help reduce the symptoms of allergies, including sneezing, itching, and runny nose, which can contribute to coughing. Common over-the-counter antihistamines include diphenhydramine (Benadryl) and cetirizine (Zyrtec). However, they can cause drowsiness, so its best to use them before bedtime or to avoid activities that require alertness, like driving. 2. Decongestants: These can help relieve nasal congestion, which can contribute to postnasal drip and cough, but they do not directly treat the cough itself. Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) is common decongestant, but it can have side effects like increased heart rate and blood pressure, so its not recommended for people with high blood pressure, heart disease, or prostate issues. 3. Cough Suppressants: These are used to suppress cough that is dry and unproductive, and they include dextromethorphan (found in many cough syrups and cold medicines). However, if your cough is productive (producing phlegm), cough suppressant may not be the best choice, as it can prevent you from clearing the mucus that your body is trying to expel. 4. Expectorants: These help loosen mucus and make it easier to cough up, and they include guaifenesin (found in Mucinex). They can be helpful if your cough is productive, but they do not address the underlying allergy. 5. Nasal Corticosteroids: These are often more effective for long-term allergy management and can help reduce inflammation in the nasal passages, which can contribute to coughing. Examples include fluticasone (Flonase) and mometasone (Nasonex), which are available by prescription. Recommendations Given the pattern of your cough, it might be beneficial to use combination of an antihistamine and decongestant, or an antihistamine and an expectorant, to manage your symptoms. However, since youve had persistent cough for an extended period, its important to consult healthcare provider to rule out other potential causes, such as respiratory infection, asthma, or acid reflux, which can also cause chronic cough. Here are some steps you can take: 1. Identify Triggers: Keep track of when your cough occurs (e.g., during certain times of the day, after being outside, or when the weather changes) to help identify potential allergens. 2. Environmental Control: Use air conditioning to keep indoor humidity low (below 50%), use dehumidifiers, and regularly clean or replace air filters to reduce mold and dust mites. 3. Allergy Testing: Consider getting allergy testing to identify specific triggers, which can help in tailoring your treatment plan, whether its through environmental control, allergy shots, or targeted medications. 4. Consult Healthcare Provider: Speak with healthcare provider, such as an allergist or primary care physician, to discuss your symptoms, undergo physical examination, and possibly undergo allergy testing, and to get prescription for appropriate medications, which might include combination of antihistamines, decongestants, and/or nasal corticosteroids, as well as advice on managing your cough, such as using humidifier, staying hydrated, and avoiding irritants like cigarette smoke and air pollution. If your cough is severe, accompanied by shortness of breath, wheezing, fever, or blood in your phlegm, or if it persists for more than 8 weeks, its crucial to seek medical attention, as these symptoms could indicate more serious condition that requires specific treatment, such as bronchitis, asthma, or even lung infection.

You are given user QUESTION and models ANSWER to it, split into numbered UNITS exact spans of the answer, in its order, under its [section] lines. The answer was graded against coverage rubric the points good answer should contain and each unit carries score in parentheses: the share of rubric credit it holds. unit that alone carries credited point scores 1.00; unit that is one of units carrying the same point scores 1/K; shares add up when unit carries several points, so score can exceed 1.00; unit that carries no credited point scores 0.00. The rubric is not shown. Your task has two steps, answered together. First, set the THRESHOLD for this answer: the lowest score unit must carry to be necessary unit the question needs. Then deduplicate among the necessary units. Rubric credit is shared by duplicates: when the answer makes point and later makes it again, both units can carry share of it. For each necessary unit in the assigned range, decide whether it duplicates an earlier necessary unit verdict remove or makes contribution of its own verdict keep. About the threshold: - The score says how much of credited point unit carries; low score means the credit for some point is spread over many units. Decide, for this question, how thin that spread may be before unit stops being necessary. - question that calls for list, set of steps or several distinct items legitimately spreads point over many units, and low threshold keeps them. question answered by few points should not have its credit spread thin, and higher threshold cuts the units that only dilute it. - Choose the threshold from the scores in front of you, reading the units themselves as the evidence of what the spread means in this answer. unit scoring 0.00 carries no credited point and is never necessary, so the threshold is greater than 0.00. - Give the threshold as decimal with two places, in the same form as the scores. unit whose score is at or above the threshold is necessary; every other unit is context only. About the units: - Each unit is an exact span of the answer, so it may lean on its neighbours or its section heading for meaning pronoun, bare list item, clause whose main verb is in the heading. Read it in that context. - Units are grouped under [section] lines carrying the answers own headings and lead-ins, in the order the answer wrote them. Those [section] lines are context only never judge them. - Units below the threshold are context only. They are never judged, and necessary unit never duplicates unit below the threshold: compare necessary units with earlier necessary units only. The principle: unit is duplicate when there is no semantically meaningful difference between what it gives the asker and what an earlier necessary unit already gave. difference is meaningful when it changes what the asker knows or can do; it is trivial when it only changes how the same thing is said shorter, longer, reworded, re-explained, emphasized, or placed under another heading. Common duplicates: the same fact, advice, item, warning or conclusion stated again in other words; the same point repeated at more length or with generic reason attached; summary, recap or conclusion that only gathers points already made; an item listed again that an earlier unit already listed; two entries of one list that make the same point under different names. Direction: the duplicate is always the later unit, never the first to make the point. Earlier means earlier in the answers order, anywhere in the answer: the comparison spans every section and reaches outside the assigned units all units are shown for that. Nothing that comes later makes an earlier unit duplicate. remove must name the earlier units number in its reasoning; if you cannot name one, the verdict is keep. When the difference is genuinely unclear, the verdict is keep. In the verdicts, do NOT judge whether the unit is true, needed, or well written the threshold has already decided what is necessary, and the rest are different evaluations. Judge as if every units content were accurate. Figure 6: Prompt for FORK (Necessity Threshold Decision) (1/2).

sections.content: Reweighted Absence-Based Rubrics (1/2) ===SYSTEM=== You are an expert evaluator. Given prompt (which may include conversation history) and generated response, please evaluate the response against EACH rubric, and state the weight each absence-based rubric item should carry. Return json object where keys are the rubric numbers (as strings) and values are objects with explanation, criteria met, type and updated weight fields. - The explanation field should be string explaining why the response does or does not meet the criteria of the rubric item. - The criteria met field should be boolean indicating whether the response meets the criteria of the rubric item. If rubric item has multiple sentences or criteria, you should consider all of them. If any of the criteria is not met, the answer should be false. Only return true if all of the criteria are met. The weight listed with an item has no bearing on this verdict: decide whether the criterion is met exactly as you would if no weight were shown. - One important exception to the above bullet point is that if criteria says such as, for example, or including, the response does not have to include all of the examples listed to meet the criteria. For example, if the criteria says Mentions practical ways to reduce household electricity use such as lowering thermostat settings, using LED bulbs, and unplugging idle devices, and the response just mentions using LED bulbs, that would still meet the criteria even though it didnt mention all of the specific examples listed in the criteria. - The type field should be presence or absence, as defined under Criterion types below. It classifies the rubric items wording, not your verdict: presence-based item that the response fails to satisfy is still presence. - The updated weight field should be an integer for an absence-based item, chosen as described under Updated weights below, and null for presence-based item. # Criterion types Each rubric item is presence-based or absence-based. The type is property of the items wording, read before looking at the response: it does not depend on the response or on whether the item is met. - presence-based item asks whether the response contains something: fact, reasoning step, list, recommendation, disclaimer, format or tone. It is met when that content appears explicitly in the response and not met when the content is missing. Missing content makes the item not met; it does not make the item absence-based. If your explanation says that the response does not mention, state or provide what the item asks for, the item is presence-based. - An absence-based item asks whether the response avoids something. Its wording forbids or limits: it does not claim, recommend, include, assume or fabricate X; it contains no errors or contradictions; it stays within limit such as only or without Y. It is met only if nothing anywhere in the response violates it, so check the whole response before marking it met, and say in the explanation what you checked for and what you found. - When rubric item has both presence requirement and an absence requirement, label it absence, even when most of the item asks for content and the prohibition or limit is single clause. Its criteria met still requires both parts to be met. - correctness word attached to specific required fact, such as correctly states that X, makes presence-based item, not an absence-based one. # Updated weights Each rubric item is listed with its weight. Rubrics like this one describe what good answer should contain in many items but what it must avoid in only few, because the ways an answer can go wrong cannot be enumerated the way its required content can. Graded as listed, such rubric rewards adding content: every extra sentence might satisfy one more presence-based item, while the few absence-based items cost little to violate, so answers grow padded and error-prone. The absence-based items are the rubrics only guards against that, and their listed weights understate that role. Beside deciding whether each item is met, your second job is to state, for each absence-based item, the weight it should carry, so that the grade favors an answer that says what is needed, says it correctly, and stops there. If it avoids the item, weigh what the answer would have lost had it not. Give the weight as an integer on the same scale as the listed weights, never below the listed weight, and as high as the case warrants. The responses own statements about what it avoids do not raise the weight. Make the scope all units when the property is not confined to one kind of unit but should be checked on every unit of the answer. - criterion is about what unit does, never about the point it makes or fails to make what the answer must contain is judged by the coverage rubric, not by your criteria. If credited unit shows the property because of the point it makes, the criterion is about content: narrow the scope or drop it. Content the question asks for is never off-topic, even when uncredited. - Write criterion only for an undesirable property you actually see in the uncredited units, and list the uncredited units that show it (uncredited only). Write as many criteria as there are distinct undesirable properties; an uncredited unit showing no such property needs no criterion, and if none does, return an empty list. - One property per criterion. Prefer several simple criteria to one that chains different properties with or; or is fine between forms of the same property (pleasantries or sign-offs). Overlap between criteria is harmless; the same property twice is not. - The grader cannot see which units are credited. criterion must never mention or depend on credit the words credit, credited, uncredited and rubric do not appear in scope or criterion. repeat is judged against earlier units of any kind: write an earlier unit, never credited unit. - Do not quote, paraphrase, number or otherwise point at units in scope or criterion: each must make sense applied to any unit of any answer to this question. - Begin with brief analysis (a few sentences): which uncredited units the answer needs and which show an undesirable property by groups, not one by one and what the latter do that the answer would be no worse without. Then write the criteria. Figure 17: Prompt for Online Criteria (1/2).

sections.content: Online Criteria (2/2) For example, for question asking what to do for someone with suspected stroke while waiting for the ambulance: - scope all units unit should not say again what an earlier unit already said, in the same or in different words. - scope units that tell the reader whom to call or where to go for help unit should not add unrequested reasons why that service is the right one beyond naming it. - scope all units unit should not explain the mechanism or types of stroke, which the question did not ask about. Not criteria: unit should mention noting the time the symptoms began. (requires point the coverage rubrics job); unit should not describe what to do while waiting. (bans what the question asks for); unit should not add steps not already covered by the credited units. (refers to credit, which the grader never sees). Output single JSON object and nothing else: json {analysis: <a few sentences: which uncredited units the answer needs, which show an undesirable property, and what those do>, criteria: [{units: [<numbers of the uncredited units that show it>], scope: <all units units that ...>, criterion: unit should not ...}]} Start your response with json and end with . Do not include any other text. ===USER=== <question> {question} </question> <answer> {units block} </answer> Write the precision rubric for this answer.
